author: reek
body: `char-at` and `char-code-at` trap on an index outside the text. This file is the half a battery can fail on: every legal index must still answer, for both builtins, because the lexer reads one of them once per source byte and a guard that refuses a legal read would stop the compiler rather than a program.

author: reek
body: The bound is tighter than `substring`'s by one. A zero-length slice at start == length is legal and answers empty; there is no byte AT index length, so `char-at s (text-length s)` traps. That one-off is the easiest thing to get wrong in either direction, so the last legal index and the first illegal one are both named here -- the legal one below, the illegal one in `codex/test/char-at-past-end.codex`.

author: reek
body: The two trap demonstrations are separate files because the two guards are separate: a negative index and an index past the end fail for different reasons and neither can stand in for the other. Both carry a `.fatal`, which means they are compile checks plus a manual read; `-Fatal` is not part of any routine battery.
